chunks: I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying:
It is permissible for the testator to retract his bequest whether he was in good health or illness.

key_terms.الْمُوصِي: the testator — the one making the bequest (wasiyya)
key_terms.وَصِيَّة: bequest — a testamentary disposition of property to take effect after death
key_terms.يَرْجِعَ: to retract/revoke — the right to withdraw or modify the bequest

ai.seo_question: Can a Muslim revoke or change his bequest (wasiyya) after making it?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the jurisprudential ruling that a testator retains the right to revoke or modify his bequest at any time — whether he is in a state of health or illness. The ruling is narrated by Ubayd ibn Zurara, a companion of Imam al-Sadiq (AS), and addresses a practical concern in Islamic inheritance law: unlike a gift that transfers ownership immediately, a bequest (wasiyya) remains revocable as long as the testator is alive. This was significant for early Muslim communities because deathbed bequests were sometimes considered irrevocable once witnessed.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Ibn Bakeyr, from Ubeyd Bin Zarara who said, 
‘I heard Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> saying
to the testator that he can retract (draw back) in his bequest whether it was during good health or illness’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from ibn Bukayr from ‘Ubayd ibn Zurarah who has narrated the following: “I once heard abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, saying,
’One who makes a will has the right to cancel or leave it, regardless of his being in good health or in illness.
